source.title: Scaling Laws for Data-Efficient Visual Transfer Learning
source.authors: Wen-Xuan Yang; Qingqv Wei; Chen-Xi Ma; Wei-Min Tan; Bo Yan

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or wrong-document issue. Some text has OCR/formatting problems and internal inconsistencies, noted under problems.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling behavior in a new setting: visual models performing downstream transfer learning, using downstream error and cross-entropy rather than language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper reports visual downstream scaling sweeps and fitted exponents. Cited findings from other studies are not recorded as results. The distillation-boundary comparisons are not rows for the listed versions because they compare distillation strategies, rather than testing the claimed power-law relationships or compute-optimal allocations.
record.test_reason: The study fits and plots power-law-plus-constant scaling of downstream error and cross-entropy for DeiT vision transformers. It varies pretraining data (64K–1.3M images), model size (about 3M–38M) and fine-tuning data. These are its own results in a new modality and a transfer regime, so they bear on V5, V6 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors claim stable power-law relations between downstream performance and pretraining data, model size and fine-tuning data, with pretraining data mattering most. Their second main conclusion is a 'distillation boundary theory': small-to-large distillation helps when data are scarce but is overtaken by standard training past a data threshold.
record.recipe_differences: Uses scaling sweeps and power-law fits, but on DeiT visual classification transfer, with downstream error/cross-entropy and fine-tuning data as factors rather than language-model held-out pretraining loss and token/compute scaling.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported fitted exponents vary across datasets; the appendix also says model-size trends can increase rather than decrease on some plotted conditions. The paper does not identify the exact curves for those increases.

fits_no_version.finding: Small-to-large distillation lowers downstream error at small pretraining data, and this advantage reverses beyond a threshold as pretraining data grows (Figures 5–6, ImageNet100 and TinyImageNet).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of small-to-large distillation shrinks and reverses as pretraining data increases.

record.problems: The reported scale ranges are modest relative to several-orders-of-magnitude scaling claims. Many trends are presented only in plots without pointwise values or uncertainty. The text describes some fitted exponents as dataset-dependent, and the appendix reports some non-decreasing model-size outcomes. Table 1 lists TinyImageNet error-rate β as 5.086, while the prose gives −5.086; Table 2 is described as having opposite signs for some parameters although the displayed values are positive. The paper also uses inconsistent model-size descriptions across sections and figures.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted from the reported scaling sweeps or fitted-exponent tables. Distillation-boundary comparisons in Figures 5–6 were left out because they compare strategies and do not measure a listed power-law or compute-optimal-allocation version.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No fit on small runs is used to predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation of parameters versus data.
Only the head count is varied, with head dimension fixed at 64. The study assumes shape matters little (citing Kaplan) and does not test it.
Image pretraining loss itself, video, and repeated data. Scale ranges span only about 1–1.3 orders of magnitude, and no goodness-of-fit is reported.
The relation between downstream performance and pretraining loss. Language-model downstream tasks.
Parameter counting, training schedule and fitting-method choices are not varied.

missing.what: Fitted coefficients E∞/L∞ and λ, ω values per dataset. Several are implausibly tiny, e.g. E∞=1.76e-27, which bears on fit reliability.
No goodness-of-fit, uncertainty, or held-out prediction is reported for any fitted law.

record.verdict_notes: The scale is small: models 3M–38M, pretraining data 64K–1.3M. Evidence is mostly plots with no fit metrics, and the internal inconsistencies (sign of β, dataset naming, threshold variable stated as pretraining versus fine-tuning data) lower confidence. This is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss and the effects of varying parameters, tokens, or compute in language models.
No test of fitting laws on small runs and predicting much larger runs.
No fixed-compute budget sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
The study varies model size by changing attention-head count; it does not compare depth, width, or other architecture shapes at a fixed parameter count.
No image/video pretraining-loss scaling test, repeated-data test, or other modalities beyond the visual classification transfer setting. The cross-entropy reported is downstream-task loss.
Tests downstream visual classification error and cross-entropy across scale, but not language-model downstream tasks or a relation between pretraining loss and downstream performance.

Shows exponent variation across datasets and reports some non-decreasing model-size curves, but does not vary parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, fitting methods, or compute-optimal allocation methods.
